Mental Health Care Plan

Patient & GP Details
- Patient: Daniel. DOB: Not recorded. Gender: Not recorded. Contact: Not recorded. Address: Not recorded.
- Referring GP: Dr Joe (consulting clinician during this consultation), Practice: Babylon. Practice Address: Not recorded. Provider No.: Not recorded. Contact: Not recorded.

Clinical Assessment

Identified Problems/Provisional Diagnoses:
- Principal: Acute situational anxiety related to current respiratory symptoms / fear of repeat severe asthma episode.
- Secondary: Panic-related hyperventilation / panic symptoms (DDx: low likelihood but consistent with patient-reported chest tightness and fear).
- Tertiary: Possible steroid-induced mood change (iatrogenic risk with prescribed oral corticosteroid; mentioned by clinician).

Clinical Details & History:
- Medications: Salbutamol (Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency not documented; Inhaled corticosteroid Clenil (Clenil Modulite) — dose/route/frequency not documented; Oral corticosteroid prescribed (type not documented) — instructed "two tablets in the morning for five days" (steroid type/name not documented). Spacer prescribed. 
- Allergies/ADRs: No drug allergies documented. Allergic history: hayfever; dust allergy. Childhood milk protein allergy.
- Past Medical History: Asthma (childhood/teen severe exacerbation requiring intubation at ~16–17); childhood eczema.

Mental Health History:
- Previous Diagnoses: Not recorded.
- Past Treatments (Therapy, Medications, Hospitalizations): Not recorded (no psychiatric treatments recorded). Past hospitalization for asthma ~age 16–17 (intubation), documented.
- Family History: Mother eczema; father asthma. No psychiatric family history recorded.

Social & Lifestyle Factors:
- Living Situation: University student; was away at university last week (specific living arrangement not recorded).
- Social Support: Not recorded.
- Occupation/Education: University student.
- Alcohol Use: Not recorded.
- Smoking/Substance Use: Not recorded.
- Key Stressors: Recent upper respiratory infection, running out of inhalers while away at university, fear of repeat severe asthma attack/intubation.

Mental Status Examination (MSE):
- Appearance & General Behaviour: Cooperative, engaged in consultation; clinically calm but reports being "scared" about recurrence of severe attack.
- Mood & Affect: Anxious/worried about respiratory status; affect congruent with stated concern.
- Speech & Thought: Speech coherent, goal-directed; no formal thought disorder documented.
- Perception: No hallucinations or perceptual disturbance reported.

Cognition:
- Orientation: Oriented to person and self (provided name and year of birth); exact full orientation to time/place not fully documented.
- Attention/Concentration: Attention and concentration appear intact during interview.
- Memory: Short- and long-term memory not formally assessed; no specific impairment reported.
- Insight & Judgement: Intact insight and judgement regarding symptoms and need for treatment (recognizes asthma likely cause; sought help).

Physical Symptoms:
- Sleep: Not recorded.
- Appetite: Not recorded.
- Motivation/Energy: Not recorded.
- Anxiety Symptoms: Reported fear/scared about repeat intubation; chest tightness described as inability to take a full breath; expresses concern and distress about current symptoms.

Risk Assessment:
- Suicidal/Self-Harm/Risk to Others: No suicidal ideation, self-harm intent or risk to others disclosed in the consultation.
- Protective Factors: Patient engaged with care, seeks treatment; prior adherence to inhalers historically; has access to medical consultation and prescriptions; family support implied (parents' medical history discussed).
- Overall Current Risk Level (Self): Low (no suicidal ideation, no self-harm, no aggressive behavior; anxiety present but patient ambulatory/not in acute psychological crisis).
- Emergency Contact: Not recorded.

Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: History of severe asthma in adolescence; atopic history (hayfever, eczema); prior hospitalization/intubation increases health-related anxiety vulnerability.
- Precipitating factors: Recent upper respiratory infection; omission/ran out of inhaled steroid and salbutamol for ~1 week while away at university leading to respiratory symptom recurrence.
- Perpetuating factors: Current chest tightness and breathlessness maintain fear and hypervigilance; being away from home and medication non-availability contribute to ongoing anxiety.
- Protective factors: Help-seeking behavior, clinician engagement, provision of acute treatments (inhalers, oral steroid, spacer), and advice on escalation.
- Integrative summary: Patient’s anxiety appears situational and temporally linked to an acute asthma exacerbation precipitated by recent URTI and medication omission. DDx rates physiological respiratory causes (acute asthma exacerbation) as primary; anxiety/panic features are present but likely secondary/reactive to respiratory symptoms. Risk of steroid-induced mood change noted as iatrogenic consideration.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem:
- Patient Goal(s): Feel safe from respiratory collapse; reduce fear of needing intubation; regain baseline breathing and reduce anxiety.
- Clinical Goal(s): Stabilize respiratory symptoms to reduce physiological trigger for anxiety; monitor and mitigate anxiety symptoms; identify any steroid-related mood changes.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Use prescribed salbutamol (Ventolin) as prescribed once dispensing available (dose/route/frequency as per prescription; patient instructed to follow label).
  - Start inhaled corticosteroid (Clenil) as prescribed when available.
  - Use spacer with inhaler as instructed when received.
  - Rest and take time off work/university as advised; self-certify for first seven days where applicable.
  - Monitor Ventolin usage; seek urgent medical attention if needing Ventolin more frequently than every 3 hours or if symptoms worsen.
  - Alert clinician if significant mood changes occur after starting oral steroids.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide prescriptions for inhaled bronchodilator and inhaled corticosteroid (arranged during consultation).
  - Provide oral corticosteroid course: instructed “two tablets in the morning for five days” (steroid type/name not documented).
  - Advise and supply spacer with instructions for use.
  - Provide safety advice: seek immediate medical attention for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain/tightness, light-headedness, or if Ventolin required more often than every 3 hours.
  - Counsel patient on possible steroid side effects including mood changes and advise monitoring.

Secondary Problem (Panic-related hyperventilation / panic symptoms):
- Patient Goal(s): Reduce acute panic sensations; manage breathlessness-related panic if it occurs.
- Clinical Goal(s): Identify and manage panic symptoms if they emerge; ensure panic does not escalate to functional impairment.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Monitor for panic symptoms (e.g., acute overwhelming fear, light-headedness, tingling, sense of unreality) and report to clinician.
  - Follow breathing/relaxation advice if provided (not documented in this consultation) and seek immediate care for severe symptoms.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Assess for panic/hyperventilation in any follow-up contacts or if anxiety symptoms persist/worsen.
  - Monitor for steroid-related mood changes that may exacerbate anxiety.
  - Consider further mental health assessment/referral if panic or anxiety symptoms persist beyond resolution of respiratory symptoms (referral not enacted in this consultation).

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Inhaler use (Ventolin PRN) and resumption of maintenance inhaler (Clenil) for ongoing control.
  - Spacer use instructions and provision of spacer.
  - Oral corticosteroid course and associated side effects (including possible mood changes, hyperglycemia, GI symptoms, headache, rash) — advised to read label and monitor.
  - When to seek urgent medical attention (worsening SOB, chest tightness/pain, light-headedness, Ventolin use > every 3 hours).
  - Recommendation to rest and take time off work/university initially.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Increasing shortness of breath at rest.
  - Need for Ventolin more frequently (e.g., more often than every 3 hours).
  - New chest pain, light-headedness, syncope.
  - New or worsening mood changes after steroid initiation.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Rest and reduce exertion while symptomatic.
  - Seek prompt medical review if symptoms escalate.
  - Monitor mood and anxiety; contact clinician if persistent or worsening.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Yes — patient agreed to prescriptions and advice during consultation.
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded.
- Review Date: Not recorded. (Patient advised to seek care urgently if worsening and to follow up as needed.)

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Anxiety / Panic-related hyperventilation — Likelihood: Low.
  - Justification: Patient reports fear and chest tightness consistent with anxiety; DDx rates anxiety as low likelihood because objective respiratory features (wheeze, cough, asthma history, missed inhalers, recent URTI) favor a physiological respiratory cause.
- Steroid-induced mood change (iatrogenic mood disturbance) — Likelihood: Low.
  - Justification: Clinician advised that oral corticosteroids can cause mood elevation or depression; this is an expected iatrogenic risk to monitor during treatment.

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pulse, blood pressure) not documented.
  - Objective respiratory examination findings and peak flow not documented.
  - Full DOB, gender, contact details, address, emergency contact not documented.
  - Smoking status and substance use history not documented.
  - Formal prior psychiatric history, prior psychological treatments, and baseline mood/anxiety severity measures not documented.
  - Specific steroid medication name not documented (dose instruction provided but medication name/type not recorded).
  - Planned follow-up appointment date/time not documented.
● Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - DDx ranks anxiety/panic as low likelihood primary cause; transcript documents notable patient fear and anxiety about repeat intubation. Conflict noted: anxiety present per transcript but DDx considers it most likely secondary to respiratory disease rather than primary psychiatric disorder.
● Transcript quality notes:
  - Some audio interruption noted during discussion of prior steroid use ("cutting in and out"); clinician and patient statements overlapping in places.
  - No vitals or objective exam data captured in transcript.
  - Some patient identifiers (exact DOB, contact) not provided in transcript.
